sources.claim: Objects delegate missing property lookup through a prototype chain, and constructor prototype properties can be shared by instances.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Every object has a hidden link to another object, its **prototype**. When you read `obj.x` and obj has no own `x`, JavaScript follows the link and looks there, then that object's prototype, and so on: the **prototype chain**. Class instances keep their **data as own properties** while **methods live once on the class prototype** and are shared. Assigning `obj.x = ...` creates an own property that **shadows** the inherited one; it never edits the prototype.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
You create 1,000 `Lesson` objects and worry that each one carries its own copy of the `summary()` method. Open DevTools and the instance shows only `title` and `minutes`. So where is summary? An instance method is found on the class prototype, while instance data remains an own property. In this lesson you'll inspect and explain a short prototype chain and a shadowed property.

```predict
{"question": "`class Lesson { constructor(t) { this.title = t; } summary() { return this.title; } } const a = new Lesson(\"A\"); const b = new Lesson(\"B\");` Is `a.summary === b.summary`?", "options": ["false, each has its own copy", "true, both find the same function on Lesson.prototype"], "answer": 1, "why": "Methods defined in a class body are stored once on Lesson.prototype. Both instances reach them through the chain."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Object records and property access**, **Function declarations, expressions and arrows**, and **Method calls and this**, because inherited methods still get this from the call site.

sections.heading: The model: own first, then follow the chain
sections.body:
```js
class Lesson {
  constructor(title) { this.title = title; }   // own data.
  summary() { return `Lesson: ${this.title}`; } // shared method.
}
const a = new Lesson("Loops");

Object.hasOwn(a, "title");                       // true
Object.hasOwn(a, "summary");                     // false
Object.getPrototypeOf(a) === Lesson.prototype;   // true
a.summary();                                     // "Lesson: Loops"

a.summary = () => "custom";                      // own property shadows it.
a.summary();                                     // "custom"
new Lesson("Maps").summary();                    // still "Lesson: Maps"
```

| Lookup of `a.summary` | Found? |
|---|---|
| 1. own properties of a. | no (until shadowed). |
| 2. Lesson.prototype. | yes, summary. |
| 3. Object.prototype. | only reached for toString and friends. |
| 4. null. | end of chain: undefined. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Does `a.summary = ...` change Lesson.prototype?", "answer": "No. Assignment creates or updates an own property on a. Other instances keep using the prototype method."}
```

examples.title: Where the method really lives
examples.situation: An instance method is found on the class prototype while instance data remains an own property of each Lesson.
walkthrough: **Inspect own data:** `Object.keys(a)` returns ["title"], so instance data remains an own property.
**Check the prototype:** `Object.hasOwn(Lesson.prototype, "summary")` is true, so the instance method is found on the class prototype.
**Compare instances:** `a.summary === b.summary` will read true because both follow the same link.
examples.result: One summary function serves every Lesson, and each instance stores only its own title.

examples.title: The shadowed price
examples.situation: A shop object inherits `discount: 0` from a defaults prototype. Code sets `item.discount = 10` for one item and a teammate fears every item now has a 10 discount.
walkthrough: The write creates an own discount property on that item only.
Other items still read discount 0 from the defaults prototype.
Check with `Object.hasOwn(item, "discount")`: true for the edited item, false for the others.
examples.result: Only the edited item shows a discount of 10; the shared default stays 0.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Every object contains a private copied version of all prototype methods.
misconceptions.correction: Instances hold only their own properties. Methods live once on the prototype and are found by following the chain at lookup time, which is why a.summary === b.summary.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Where the method really lives", which keys did Object.keys(a) show?

analogy.example: A prototype chain is like asking for a stapler at work: first you check **your own desk**, then the **team cupboard**, then the **office store room**. You don't each own a stapler; you borrow the shared one. Putting your own stapler on your desk means you stop looking further.
usefulFor: shadowing = your own stapler on your desk
limitations: Borrowed staplers move; prototype methods stay put and run with your this.
The chain ends at null, like a store room with no door beyond it.

steps.explanation: The constructor stores title as instance data on a.
The instance method is found on the class prototype.

trace.textAlternative: Following a short prototype chain. Step 1, Create: own keys of a is ['title']. The constructor stores title as instance data on a. Step 2, Lookup: a has summary? is no; found on is Lesson.prototype. The instance method is found on the class prototype. Step 3, Shadow: own keys of a is ['title', 'summary']; Lesson.prototype.summary is unchanged. Assigning creates an own property that shadows the shared method.

remediation.explanation: For any property read ask: **Is it own? If not, which prototype has it?** For any write: **it lands on the object itself.** Use Object.hasOwn and Object.getPrototypeOf to check instead of guessing.

recap.summary: To inspect and explain a short prototype chain, remember that reads check own properties first and then follow the prototype link, class methods live once on the prototype, and a write creates an own property that shadows the inherited one without changing the prototype.
